resources.string: How a type A intercalated cell helps excrete acid
One type A intercalated cell in a normal cortical collecting duct. The drawing shows directions of movement, not amounts or rates. Structures and particles are not to scale.

The apical side of the type A intercalated cell faces the duct lumen. Its basolateral side faces the tissue between the duct and nearby blood vessels. Neighboring principal cells mainly handle salt and water.
An apical proton pump (H⁺-ATPase) moves hydrogen ions (H⁺) from the type A cell into the tubular fluid. Type B intercalated cells differ: they can secrete bicarbonate into the lumen.

On the opposite side, the AE1 exchanger moves bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) out of the cell in exchange for chloride. Bicarbonate passes through the space between the duct and nearby capillary on its way back to the blood.
In tubular fluid, a proton can bind to ammonia to form ammonium (NH₄⁺). Hydrogen phosphate can also take up a proton, forming dihydrogen phosphate (H₂PO₄⁻).
Ammonium and protonated phosphate travel downstream in the tubular fluid and leave in urine, carrying acid out of the body. Meanwhile, bicarbonate from the type A cell returns toward the blood.
